academic_response: A pin tumbler lock is a toleranced spring-loaded alignment system rather than a perfectly discrete one. Inside the lock plug are vertical pin stacks consisting of key pins in the plug, driver pins above them, and springs pushing the stacks downward. When no key is inserted, the driver pins straddle the shear line preventing rotation. When the correct key is inserted, each key cut lifts a pin stack to a precise height aligning every gap between key pins and driver pins exactly on the shear line. The fundamental mechanical weakness is tolerance stacking — real locks have slightly different pin diameters, chamber alignments, spring strength variation, and wear over time. This creates a condition where not all pins bind equally when torque is applied, and the system unintentionally leaks information about internal alignment through differential mechanical resistance.

The plug can only rotate when the gap between the key pins and driver pins lines up exactly at the shear line. A pick is then used to lift pins one by one in binding order until all pins are set at the shear line and the plug rotates.
